universalAnswers.whatHappened: Women accounted for 26% of U.S. hires into AI occupations in 2025, compared with 50% of hires into other occupations, according to research LinkedIn published on August 18. Its separate international leadership analysis found that women held 13% of top executive AI leadership roles at AI companies. These figures describe who is getting hired and who holds authority.A U.S. Census Bureau report published on August 11 measures something different: how often people use AI at work. Among workers who had used AI for at least one of the tasks surveyed, 30% of men and 17% of women reported using it every day in the previous week. The survey was conducted in March 2026.Those are different groups and different questions. The hiring figures do not cover every job in which someone uses AI. The frequency figures do not measure skill, interest or whether daily use would help someone do her job. Neither report establishes why a particular woman has less access to an opportunity.
universalAnswers.plainLanguageIdentity: Separate findings on who holds AI jobs and how often AI users use it at work.
universalAnswers.evidenceBasis: LinkedIn August18 platform analysis and U.S. Census August11 March2026 survey reporting.
universalAnswers.evidenceLimits: Separate groups; descriptive outcomes do not establish individual ability, motivation or causes.
universalAnswers.readerRelevance: Workplace access, paid time and fair project selection shape opportunities a reader can ask about.
universalAnswers.affectedPeople: Women in AI hiring and leadership; separately U.S. workers who had used AI at work.
universalAnswers.changesNow: Historical August findings; correction changes our framing, not the underlying labour market.
universalAnswers.uncertainty: The reports do not identify reasons for each individual outcome; no personal career forecast.
universalAnswers.readerAction: Readers can ask to participate in learning and decisions, and ask questions without arriving as experts.
universalAnswers.betterQuestion: Who is responsible for providing supported access and how are project participants selected?

work-economy.affectedWorkers: U.S. AI occupation hires in2025, international executive roles at AI companies, U.S. AI users at work in March2026.
work-economy.evidenceScale: LinkedIn platform data is not every worker; Census self-reported task use. Do not combine denominators.
work-economy.currentVsForecast: Historical reported findings; no future jobs or career-outcome prediction.
work-economy.distribution: Gender findings explicit; no race, income or disability effect inferred.
work-economy.gainsAndLosses: Representation and frequency measured; individual pay gains, motives and harms not inferred.
work-economy.readerOptions: Employers make opportunities visible, provide time and support, and welcome questions; readers can ask to participate.

translation.newsVersionExact: “These reports show gaps in AI hiring, leadership and daily workplace use. They do not show that women lack interest or ability. Employers need to examine who gets the tools, learning time and opportunities to take part.”
translation.actualMeaningExact: Those are different groups and different questions.
translation.mechanismExact: If a manager selects a team to test a new AI tool only from people already using it, someone who never had supported access can miss another opportunity.

jargon.plainMeaning: how often people use AI at work

learningConnections.concept: Interpreting workplace statistics without inferring causes
learningConnections.learningPayoff: Ask who was measured and what the research can establish.
learningConnections.trigger: When a specific evidence-versus-cause lesson is admitted for this route
